summary: Astronauts in space are not really weightless; they float because they and their spacecraft are constantly falling together around Earth, and this changes their bodies and daily routines.
introduce: Show the three key terms on the board and ask students to rate each one: “I know it,” “I have seen it,” or “It is new.” Tell them to watch for these words in “Zero Gravity: Why Astronauts Float” and use clues around them to understand their meaning.

keyTerms.def: the curving path a spacecraft or planet follows as it travels around another object
a condition in which gravity is still present but people and objects feel almost weightless
a liquid, such as blood or water, that can flow or shift from one place to another

challengeTerms.def: happening all the time without stopping
relating to the inner-ear system that helps the body sense balance
the upward force that makes an object float or feel lighter in water

discussion: Do you agree or disagree that astronauts in space feel no gravity at all? Use evidence from the article to explain.
Choose one way that microgravity changes the human body.
struggling: Pre-teach orbit, microgravity, and fluid with pictures or gestures, then let weak readers draw a quick picture for each term and use it in a short spoken sentence.
gifted: Challenge advanced readers to use continuous, vestibular, and buoyancy in a short paragraph that teaches the class one of the terms with their own example.
